newsitem.title: JORDAN: Hamas warns Arafat against "dangerous" crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Hamas warns Arafat against "dangerous" crackdown.

text.p: The Islamic resistance group Hamas warned Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Monday against heeding Israeli demands for a crackdown on its supporters, saying it would unleash deep Palestinian anger.
"It would be dangerous, not just for him...It would lead to Palestinians fighting Palestinians," Hamas spokesman Ibrahim Ghoshe said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has demanded that Arafat crush militant opponents of his interim peace deal with Israel as a precondition to resuming negotiations after a double suicide bombing in Jerusalem.

Netanyahu said on Sunday there was a "growing indication" that Hamas was behind the July 30 attack which killed 13 people as well as the bombers. The attack was the deadliest in Israel for over a year.

Arafat has argued that the bombers probably came from abroad, in a defence against sanctions imposed by Israel on Palestinian areas after the bombing and charges from Netanyahu that he has failed to crack down on Moslem militants.
Ghoshe declined to comment on who carried out the attack but said Arafat, who responded to similar bombings last year with a wave of arrests, was in no position to get tough this time.

He said Palestinians were embittered that they had gained little from their 1993 interim self-rule deal with Israel, which Hamas opposes, and were losing faith in the Palestinian Authority after reports of rampant corruption.

"The behaviour of the Palestinian people will not be the same as it was one and a half years ago," said Ghoshe, spokesman for Hamas's exiled leadership. "The Palestinian community is angry with the Palestinian Authority for many reasons."
Ghoshe said Arafat had been given a list of 30 names of people Israel wanted handed over and a further 150 it wanted arrested. He did not say where his information came from.
Arafat has responded to Netanyahu's demands by calling for a lifting of Israel's closure of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, which he said amounted to "state terrorism".

U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross has been holding separate talks with Netanyahu and Arafat to try to bridge their differences, but has said his efforts were focused primarily on addressing Israel's call for security cooperation.
The crisis between the two sides sparked off a flurry of consultations last week, including a visit to Amman by Arafat during which he met leading Hamas figure Musa Abu Marzook.
Abu Marzook, detained in the United States for two years without charge, was deported to Jordan in May after Israel dropped its extradition charges against him.
"It was a personal visit, nothing more," Ghoshe said. "Arafat wanted to offer his congratulations on Abu Marzook's release."
